questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sample cannot prove a universal claim
questions.stem: Explain why no sample, however large, can prove that every rider's wait is under 10 minutes.

answer.exemplar: A sample only observes some riders, so an unobserved rider could exceed 10 minutes. Sampling cannot cover the entire population with certainty, so universal claims remain unsupported by data alone.

questions.explanation: Samples omit part of the population, so a counterexample may exist unobserved. Universal claims need full enumeration, not sampling.
questions.hint: A sample cannot observe everyone.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain empirical rule applicability
questions.stem: When is the empirical rule least reliable?

options.text: For data with a small standard deviation
For data with a large sample size
For heavily skewed or bimodal data
For data with a large mean

questions.explanation: The rule assumes a normal bell shape. Skew or bimodality breaks that, making percentages unreliable. Size, spread, and location do not.
questions.hint: Shape, not size or scale, matters.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why conditional probabilities differ
questions.stem: Explain why P(rain|delay) and P(delay|rain) are generally different.

answer.exemplar: They condition on different events and use different denominators. P(delay|rain) divides by rainy days, while P(rain|delay) divides by delayed trips, so their values and meanings differ unless base rates align.

questions.explanation: The two conditionals reverse the roles of rain and delay, changing denominators. Their values differ unless the base rates coincide.
questions.hint: Check which event is the condition.
